children.text: X-ray jets from active galactic nuclei

Use the historical one-dimensional steady jet model. Distance s is measured from the active galactic nucleus (AGN), cross-section A=πr², speed v, Lorentz factor γ, and proper particle density n. Material is injected at rest in the AGN frame at uniform mass rate α per volume. Mean rest mass per particle is μpp=0.59mp, and the supplied effective energy/enthalpy per particle is εav=μpp c²+13P/(4n). Treat its energy-flux prescription as the given model. For Centaurus A take jet power Pj=\(10^{36}\) W, s1=252 pc, r1=30 pc, v1=0.667c, s2=5.94 kpc, r2=500 pc, v2=0.52c, and a straight conical boundary between these ends. External pressure is P(s)=\(5.7\times10^{-12}\)(s/1 kpc)^−1.5 Pa. Use 1 pc=\(3.086\times10^{16}\) m and c=\(3.00\times10^{8}\) m/s. Later sections use an isotropic ultrarelativistic electron gas with proper differential density f(ε)dε and positive electron charge magnitude e. Source discrepancies are explained in the worked solution rather than silently enforced as grading keys.

Given observations: Cen A AX1C and BX2 fade by 23% and 15% over 15 years with no X-ray spectral change. M87 HST-1 and Knot A fade by 73% and 12% over 5 years with unchanged brightness in lower-frequency bands and no X-ray spectral data. Choose the more likely of adiabatic expansion and synchrotron cooling for each, citing previous reasoning. Use \(j(\nu)\propto B^{(1+p)/2}\nu^{(1-p)/2}\).

children.text: X-ray jets from active galactic nuclei
Longitudinal lengths contract by 1/γ while particle number and transverse area are invariant. Thus \(n^{\prime}=\gamma n\).
The swept volume per time is Av, so \(F_p=\gamma nAv\).
Injected particle rate is αV/μpp, hence \(\gamma_2n_2A_2v_2-\gamma_1n_1A_1v_1=\alpha V/\mu_{pp}\).

Each particle's model energy transforms by γ, while the number flux has another γ. Thus \(F_E=\gamma^2nAv\epsilon_{av}\). Material injected at rest adds only rest energy, so \(F_E(s_2)-F_E(s_1)=\alpha Vc^2\).
Energy injection is αVc² and rest-mass flux increases by αV. Their contributions cancel in Pj for any segment. Thus \(dP_j/ds=0\).

Rearrange \(P_j=(\gamma-1)\dot Mc^2+(13/4)\gamma^2AvP\): \[\dot M=\frac{P_j-(13/4)\gamma^2AvP}{(\gamma-1)c^2}.\] Substitution gives approximately \(2.8\times10^{19}\) kg/s and \(5.2\times10^{19}\) kg/s at the inlet and outlet. The displayed inputs support only about two significant figures.

The model momentum flux is \(\Pi(s)=F_E(s)v(s)/c^2=[P_j+\dot M(s)c^2]v(s)/c^2\). The net increase is Π2−Π1, approximately \(2.01\times10^{27}\) N with the supplied numerical inputs. The source quotes \(1.9\times10^{27}\) N after rounding. The phrase total momentum flux in this task refers to this difference, not either endpoint alone.

The end forces are P1A1−P2A2. The sloping wall contributes an outward axial component, giving \[F_{Pr}=P_1A_1-P_2A_2+\int_{r_1}^{r_2}2\pi rP[s(r)]\,dr,\quad s(r)=s_1+\frac{s_2-s_1}{r_2-r_1}(r-r_1).\] The integral is about \(9.71\times10^{26}\) N and the net force about \(8.10\times10^{26}\) N with the supplied inputs. The source rounds these to \(9.8\times10^{26}\) N and \(8.2\times10^{26}\) N.

The model would require Π=FPr. With the quoted rounded results, \(|1.9-0.82|/0.82\times100\%\simeq132\%\). Direct calculation before rounding gives about 148% from Π≈\(2.01\times10^{27}\) N and FPr≈\(8.10\times10^{26}\) N. The source prints 40%, inconsistent with both its stated denominator and its displayed numbers. Use the defined denominator and show your arithmetic.
\[u=U/V=\int_0^\infty\epsilon f(\epsilon)\,d\epsilon.\] Physical distributions must have cutoffs or decay sufficiently rapidly for this integral to exist.

A particle incident at θ carries normal momentum (ε/c)cosθ and reverses it. The incident flux includes c cosθ and solid-angle weight sinθ dθdφ/(4π). Integrating the incident hemisphere gives \[\frac{\Delta p_z}{\Delta t}=\frac{\Delta A}{3}\int_0^\infty\epsilon f(\epsilon)d\epsilon.\] The gas momentum change is opposite to the force on the wall.
Divide the wall force by area to obtain P=u/3, or \(U=3PV\).
With no heat input, dU=−P dV. Since U=3PV, \(3VdP+4PdV=0\). Integrate to get \(PV^{4/3}=\text{constant}\).

The perpendicular speed is v sinφ. Force balance is \(eBv\sin\phi=\gamma m\Omega_gv\sin\phi\), giving \(\Omega_g=eB/(\gamma m)\), independent of nonzero pitch. The speed of the unit velocity vector on the direction sphere is \(\Omega_g\sin\phi\). The source calls the latter Ω but labels it gyration frequency. The distinction is needed to retain the correct pitch dependence.

The emission direction traverses an angular width 2/γ at rate Ωg sinφ, so emission duration is \(2/(\gamma\Omega_g\sin\phi)\). Arrival-time compression is of order 1−v/c≈1/(2γ²). Thus \[\Delta t_{obs}\sim\frac{m}{\gamma^2eB\sin\phi}.\] Numerical cone factors are approximate. The source's pitch-independent result corresponds to sinφ≈1 and should not be applied at arbitrary pitch.

\[\nu_{chr}\sim1/\Delta t_{obs}\sim\gamma^2eB\sin\phi/m.\] This is a characteristic inverse width, not the gyrofrequency in cycles per second. A precise spectral-peak calculation supplies additional numerical factors.
\(\tau=E/P_s=6\pi\epsilon_0m^4c^5/[e^4B^2E\sin^2\phi]\). It is an instantaneous loss timescale, decreasing with energy.

Linear dimensions scale as (V/V0)^(1/3), and any material area as (V/V0)^(2/3). Conserved flux gives \(B=B_0(V/V_0)^{-2/3}\). The relevant flux is through a material cross-section, not the identically zero net flux through a closed surface.

Let a=V/V0. From U∝V^(−1/3), each energy scales as ε=ε0 a^(−1/3). Conservation in an energy bin gives \(Vf(\epsilon)d\epsilon=V_0f_0(\epsilon_0)d\epsilon_0\). Therefore \[f(\epsilon)=\kappa_0a^{-(p+2)/3}\epsilon^{-p}.\] The energy bounds scale by a^(−1/3). The source's a^−1 normalization omits the energy-bin Jacobian and energy shift, and integrates an unbounded power law that need not converge. The slope stays p but its normalization is not simple number dilution.

For fixed field and pitch, \(\dot\epsilon=-a_s\epsilon^2\), so \(\epsilon(t)=\epsilon_i/(1+a_s\epsilon_it)\) and loss time is 1/(as εi). Higher energies cool faster. An initially finite power-law population develops a high-energy cutoff or break rather than preserving its original spectrum. For an impulsive population, \(f(\epsilon,t)=\kappa\epsilon^{-p}(1-a_st\epsilon)^{p-2}\) below the evolving cutoff, so p>2 gives progressive high-energy suppression. A universal slope increase for every p or injection history cannot be inferred from the loss law alone.

Adiabatic expansion preserves the power-law slope while reducing field and density, favouring it for AX1C and BX2. Synchrotron cooling preferentially affects the highest-energy electrons and their X-rays, favouring it for HST-1 and Knot A because their lower-frequency brightness is unchanged. These are comparative interpretations within the two mechanisms posed, not unique exclusions of all possible astrophysical causes.
